video_title: Building our piece of the electric stack
gist: David Roberts talks with Impulse Labs founder Sam D'Amico (co-author of 'The Electric Slide') about the electric stack — batteries, motors, power electronics, chips — which is ~99% cheaper since 1990 and mostly made in China. D'Amico argues the US should use the AI data-center boom to reindustrialize, explains battery-buffered appliances (10 kW per burner on 120 V) and Impulse's shift to licensing its platform, and predicts AI demand will electrify the whole economy within a decade.

themes.theme: The electric stack and its cost curves

insights.claim: The electric stack — batteries, electric motors, chips and power electronics — has gotten about 99% cheaper since 1990, which is why cars, drones, boats and stoves keep going electric.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Ongoing cost declines expand the addressable market for electrified devices.
insights.quote: that electric stack has gotten about 99% cheaper since 1990

insights.claim: China manufactures most of the electric stack, including roughly three quarters of the world's lithium-ion batteries and 90% of the magnets that spin motors.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: US electrification supply chains are structurally dependent on China.
insights.quote: roughly 3/4 of the world's lithium-ion batteries and 90% of the magnets that spin the motors

insights.claim: D'Amico argues the four stack technologies are the first fully coherent set addressable by software, and that Tesla's Model S being built like a consumer electronics device was as revolutionary as being an EV.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Software-defined hardware is the competitive frontier in electrified products.

insights.claim: Tesla was enabled by cheap 18650 laptop battery cells already in scale production; afterwards the EV industry itself drove further battery cost declines.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Adjacent-market scale is what unlocks new electrified categories.
insights.quote: Laptops effectively enabled an electric sports car.

insights.claim: Gallium nitride and silicon carbide power electronics now enable close to 20 kW per rack unit in data centers and solid-state transformer work by companies like Heron Power and Vicor.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: GaN/SiC power electronics are a key enabler of AI data-center power density.
insights.quote: close to 20 kilowatts in like single unit of rack space

insights.claim: D'Amico argues neodymium magnets have improved materially over 24 years, and that the rare-earth supply chain was ignored in the US until EVs and now robotics made it strategic.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Rare-earth and motor supply chains are a policy and investment focus.

insights.claim: D'Amico expects a 'ChatGPT moment' for robotics soon, driving demand for US-built motors and actuators; he discloses being an investor in one such company.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Domestic motor/actuator makers stand to benefit from a robotics wave.

insights.claim: The 'Electric Slide' essay argues that while America bets on AI, China is betting on the hardware, and China has made the smarter bet.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Electric-stack manufacturing may be the more durable strategic asset than frontier AI.
insights.quote: While America is betting the future on AI, China is betting on the hardware, and China has made the smarter bet.

insights.claim: D'Amico says the US is missing an opportunity to use tens to hundreds of gigawatts of planned data center buildout — much of it electric-stack-shaped hardware — to reindustrialize, partly because AI hardware is intentionally not tariffed.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: AI capex is flowing offshore rather than anchoring US factories.

insights.claim: D'Amico predicts a bimodal split in AI winners between those who control electric-stack technologies and the AI labs.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Physical infrastructure owners may capture AI value alongside model labs.
insights.quote: maybe there's going to be a bimodal split in the winners of the AI race

insights.claim: Although Grok is not the preferred model versus Claude and Codex, Musk's ability to plug data centers into power and build large coherent clusters gives him leverage over other AI players.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Power and build capacity can matter more than model quality in the AI race.
insights.quote: People are preferring Claude and Codex to Grok in a lot of cases for now.

insights.claim: The US banned new foreign-sourced power inverters on network security grounds, an action D'Amico likens to the Cisco/Huawei disputes and says has had bipartisan reception.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Grid-connected power electronics face a domestic-sourcing tailwind.

insights.claim: D'Amico argues co-location of engineers and factories in Shenzhen speeds iteration so much that founders spend two months there to get first prototypes, effectively a 'matter compiler'.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: China's prototyping ecosystem is a compounding innovation advantage.
insights.quote: Shenzhen is turning into this like what I would call like a matter compiler.

insights.claim: Apple compensates for design-manufacturing separation by flying engineers business class to factories, reportedly around $100 million a year on United alone.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Only megacaps can afford to bridge the design-factory gap.

insights.claim: SpaceX's vertical integration was forced by the absence of a supply base for 10,000 satellites a year and ITAR barring use of Asian contract manufacturers; Tesla is less vertical than assumed and uses Asian contract manufacturers for many PCBs.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Vertical integration is often a supply-base necessity rather than a philosophy.

insights.claim: D'Amico says making printed circuit boards in California is effectively illegal due to CARB and water agency rules on electroplating, and calls for environmental reform to 'legalize green jobs'.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Permitting/environmental rules are a binding constraint on US hardware reshoring.

insights.claim: D'Amico argues the US needs baseline volume production of replacement-level basics, likening the US to WWII Germany with wonder weapons but no volume, and says drone motor demand from Ukraine alone may not support a domestic industry.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Defense demand alone won't sustain domestic electric-stack manufacturing.

insights.claim: D'Amico says consumer demand must anchor industrial policy, supported by cheap factory financing, state tax abatements and workforce incentives that mimic China's provincial competition.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: State-level incentive competition is a lever for US manufacturing.
insights.quote: The consumer demand is the industrial policy we need to be, you know, architecting.

insights.claim: D'Amico thinks the US should allow BYD, Geely and Xiaomi to sell cars in the US even though it would be a Sputnik moment showing how far behind the Big Three are; he says Ford's Jim Farley understands the problem.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Chinese EV entry would pressure Detroit incumbents hard.

insights.claim: Roberts argues current US EV policy is the opposite of what taking the electric stack seriously would require, protecting combustion past its shelf life.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Policy is misaligned with electrification economics.

insights.claim: Impulse Labs' induction cooktop has a built-in battery that lets it push 10 kW per burner while plugging into an ordinary 120 V outlet.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Battery buffering removes panel/service upgrade barriers to electrification.
insights.quote: push 10 kW per burner while plugging into an ordinary 120 V outlet

insights.claim: Induction cooktops use about 200-300 Wh per day per the EIA but peak at 7-10 kW, so huge panel capacity is wired for a device that uses less energy than a computer.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Peak-to-average mismatch is the core economic case for appliance batteries.

insights.claim: D'Amico argues nearly every machine — ovens, dryers, water heaters, CNC machines, data centers — has a big peak-to-average power gap that batteries can buffer, with HVAC the main exception needing ~4 hours of storage.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Battery-buffered power modules have a very large addressable market.
insights.quote: I think it's pretty much everything.

insights.claim: Storage turns the grid from a single synchronized 'rotating shaft' into an internet-like self-healing network with packet buffers at every layer, a transition D'Amico says is only partway done.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Distributed storage at every layer is a long-run grid architecture trend.

insights.claim: Impulse is licensing its core electronics platform to bigger appliance brands for cooktops and ranges at various price points, aiming to be 'Intel plus Microsoft' for induction appliances, while still making the electronics itself.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: The business model is shifting from a $7,000 niche product to platform licensing.
insights.quote: it's also like Intel plus Microsoft is probably the way to think about it

insights.claim: The Impulse cooktop contains a UL 1741-compliant bidirectional inverter that is not yet enabled; distributed in-appliance batteries avoid partial-home-backup installation complexity and can be aggregated for virtual power plants.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Appliance batteries could become VPP assets without costly home-battery installs.

insights.claim: D'Amico argues utilities capture most of the value of distributed batteries because they avoid transmission upgrades, with other structures merely sharing that value.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: VPP economics hinge on utility compensation structures.

insights.claim: Impulse's next targets include industrial equipment like CNC machines, where power buffering lets more machines fit in a building, via a repeatable core module of battery, power electronics and software.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Industrial power buffering is a reshoring-adjacent opportunity.

insights.claim: D'Amico believes most people underestimate AI because only about 2% of Americans pay for ChatGPT, while frontier labs are throwing thousands of agents at problems like math proofs.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Public perception lags frontier AI capability.

insights.claim: D'Amico predicts AI-driven demand will buy more batteries and solar than ever, because gas turbines are bottlenecked by hard materials problems while solar is not.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Turbine supply constraints favor solar-plus-storage for data center power.
insights.quote: gas turbines are fundamentally bottlenecked by hard materials problems

insights.claim: D'Amico predicts the entire economy will be electric within roughly 10 years driven by demand pull from robotics, autonomy and data centers, noting the Cybertruck has electric brakes with no hydraulics.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Electrification may be driven by autonomy and robotics rather than climate policy.
insights.quote: the entire economy is going to be electric within the next 10 years, period

insights.claim: D'Amico expects stratospheric aerosol geoengineering to become the 'spicy topic' within about 10 years as warming worsens into the 2040s-2050s, and says some in tech are confident it will work.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Geoengineering could become a policy and investment theme.

insights.claim: D'Amico contends Silicon Valley hasn't stopped caring about climate; the language changed but the reindustrialization agenda uses the same tech stack once anointed for climate.
insights.speaker: Sam D'Amico
insights.so_what: Reindustrialization rhetoric still drives clean-tech deployment.
insights.quote: the language has changed, but I'm not sure if the mission has changed
